chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Isma'il ibn Mihran, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, from Abu Maryam al-Ansari, from Abu Ja'far (AS), who said:

A man from al-Basra stood up before Amir al-Momineen (AS) and said: 'O Amir al-Momineen (AS)! Inform us about the brethren.' So he (AS) said: 'The brethren are of two types – the trustworthy brethren and the friendly brethren.'

As for the trustworthy brethren, they are the palm, the wing, the family, and the wealth. So when you are with a brother of yours who is at the limit of trustworthiness, then spend your wealth and your body for him, be sincere to those who are sincere to him, and be an adversary to those who are his adversaries, and conceal his secrets and his faults, and manifest the good that is in him. And know, O questioner, that they are scarcer than red sulfur.

And as for the friendly brethren, you attain your pleasure from them, so do not sever that from them, nor seek what lies beyond that from their consciences; and exert for them what they exert for you of a cheerful countenance and a sweet tongue.'

key_terms.إِخْوَانُ الثِّقَةِ: Trustworthy brethren – those with whom the bond of true trust has been established, obligating full commitment of wealth, body, loyalty, and the guarding of their secrets and faults
key_terms.إِخْوَانُ الْمُكَاشَرَةِ: Friendly brethren – those with whom one maintains pleasant outward social interaction, without entailing the deeper obligations of sincere brotherhood
key_terms.الثِّقَةُ: Trustworthiness/trust – the defining quality that elevates a social relationship to the highest rank of brotherhood, warranting total devotion
key_terms.الضَّمِيرُ: Conscience/inner self – the private inner convictions and hidden intentions that one must not probe or demand access to in the case of friendly brethren
key_terms.الْجَنَاحُ: The wing – a metaphor for the sheltering, elevating, and encompassing care that the trustworthy brother provides
key_terms.الْكَفُّ: The palm – a metaphor for the practical protection, support, and outstretched help that the trustworthy brother provides
key_terms.الْكِبْرِيتُ الْأَحْمَرُ: Red sulfur (al-kibrit al-ahmar) – a classical Arabic proverb denoting something of extreme and legendary rarity, here applied to the scarcity of truly trustworthy brethren
key_terms.طَلَاقَةُ الْوَجْهِ: Cheerfulness of the countenance – the open, pleasant facial expression that constitutes the appropriate currency of exchange in friendly social relations

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali (AS) say about the two types of brothers and friends in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam 'Ali (AS), responding to a question posed in al-Basra as reported by Imam Abu Ja'far (AS), divides human brethren into two categories: the trustworthy brethren (ikhwan al-thiqa), who are as rare as red sulfur and toward whom one must devote wealth, body, loyalty, and the guarding of secrets; and the friendly brethren (ikhwan al-mukashara), with whom one maintains cordial social pleasantries without expecting or demanding deeper commitment. This hadith establishes a refined ethical framework for navigating human relationships, distinguishing sincere brotherhood from mere social affability.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Khalid, from Ismail Bin Mihran, from Yunus Bin Yaqoub, from Abu Maryam Al Ansary, (It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’farasws having said: ‘A man from Al-Basra stood up to Amir Al-Momineenasws and he said, ‘O Amir Al-Momineenasws!
Inform us about the brethren’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The brethren are of two types – The trustworthy brethren and the friendly brethren.

So as for the trustworthy brethren, so they are the palm, and the wing, and the family and the wealth. So when you were with a brother of yours who was upon the limit of trustworthiness, so spend the wealth and (exert) your body for him, and be sincere to those who are sincere to him, and assist those who assist him, and conceal his secrets and his faults and manifest the goodness from him. And know, O you people! They are scarcer than the red Ruby (in nature).

And as for the friendly brethren, so you would be attaining your pleasure from them, therefore do no cut that off from them, nor seek what is behind that from their consciences, and exert for them what they are exerting for you, from the relaxedness of the face and the sweetness of the tongue’.
en.sarwar: 3. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from Isma’il ibn Mehran from Yunus ibn Ya’qub from abu Maryam al-Ansari from abu Ja’far (a.s.) who has said the following:

“Once a man in Basra stood before Amir al-Mu’minin (Ali ibn abu Talib) (a.s.) and asked, ‘O Amir al-Mu’minin, speak to us of brothers (in belief).’ The Imam said, ‘Brothers are of two kinds: Trustworthy brothers and smiling brothers.

The trustworthy brothers are one’s palms, wings, the family and wealth. If they are trustworthy you may spend and work for them, be sincere to those sincere to him, and be the enemy of his enemies, conceal his secrets and faults and publicize his virtuous qualities. You (questioning person) must know that they are as rare as alchemy.

On the other hand, you may enjoy the smiling brother’s association that you should not cut it off from them but do not seek anything beyond it of their conscience. Do for them as much as they do for you like a happy face and sweet expressions.’”
